12. Compressed Sensing

CNRS & DMA, École Normale Supérieure

Chapter PDF · Complete book

Compressed sensing aims to recover sparse signals from far fewer measurements than their ambient dimension. This can reduce acquisition costs when measurements are expensive, but success depends on how the sensing operator interacts with the signal representation. Motivated by the single-pixel camera, we analyze recovery from random measurements, distinguish guarantees for fixed signals from uniform guarantees, and extend the discussion to structured Fourier sampling.

Hardware constraints often prevent direct implementation of an ideal random matrix. The theory nevertheless guides the design of structured acquisition schemes, whose physical assumptions and computational costs must be considered separately.

The main references for this chapter are [23, 21, 29].

12.1 Motivation and Potential Applications¶

12.1.1 Single-Pixel Camera¶

The “single-pixel camera” developed at Rice University [18] motivates compressed acquisition. Figure 12.1 illustrates the reconstruction principle with simulated measurements of a flower image.

A central idea is to combine acquisition and compression in a single device. Conventional acquisition first samples the analog scene f~0\tilde f_0f~​0​ at high resolution to obtain an image f0∈RQf_0\in\mathbb{R}^Qf0​∈RQ, then compresses it to MMM significant coefficients using (5.3). Compressed acquisition instead records a vector y∈RPy\in\mathbb{R}^Py∈RP directly. The aim is to keep the measurement count PPP close to the sparsity level MMM, typically with a logarithmic overhead, while retaining enough information for accurate reconstruction.

The scene f~0\tilde f_0f~​0​ is modeled as a light-intensity function. Its value f~0(s)\tilde f_0(s)f~​0​(s) gives the intensity at position s∈R2s \in \mathbb{R}^2s∈R2 in the camera’s focal plane.

Light is focused onto an array of QQQ micromirrors in the focal plane. Each mirror directs light either toward the sensor or away from it; the mirrors themselves record no information.

The device cycles rapidly through PPP mirror configurations. For p=1,…,Pp=1,\ldots,Pp=1,…,P, the entry Φp,q∈{0,1}\Phi_{p,q}\in\{0,1\}Φp,q​∈{0,1} indicates whether mirror qqq is off or on during exposure ppp.

A single sensor integrates the light directed toward it during each exposure, producing one measurement yp∈Ry_p\in\mathbb{R}yp​∈R.

Let cqc_qcq​ be the region occupied by mirror qqq in the focal plane, and define its integrated intensity by f0,q=∫cqf~0(s) dsf_{0,q}=\int_{c_q}\tilde f_0(s)\,\mathrm{d}sf0,q​=∫cq​​f~​0​(s)ds. The discrete image f0∈RQf_0\in\mathbb{R}^Qf0​∈RQ and the measurements y∈RPy\in\mathbb{R}^Py∈RP are then related by

∀ p=1,…,P,yp≈∑q=1QΦp,q∫cqf~0(s)ds=(Φf0)p,\forall \,p = 1,\ldots,P, \quad y_p \approx \sum_{q=1}^Q \Phi_{p,q} \int_{c_q} \tilde f_0(s) \text{d} s = (\Phi f_0)_p,∀p=1,…,P,yp​≈q=1∑Q​Φp,q​∫cq​​f~​0​(s)ds=(Φf0​)p​,

The symbol ≈\approx≈ accounts for acquisition noise. We therefore use the usual inverse-problem model

y=Φf0+w∈RPy = \Phi f_0 + w \in \mathbb{R}^Py=Φf0​+w∈RP

where www is the noise vector.

The intermediate image f0f_0f0​ is never recorded: the device measures yyy directly from the analog scene f~0\tilde f_0f~​0​.

Binary mirror patterns are not centered random variables. Centered signed measurements can be formed by subtracting an appropriate total-intensity measurement or by differencing complementary exposures, followed by normalization. This distinction matters when applying the random-matrix assumptions below.

Recovering the ideal discrete image f0f_0f0​ from yyy requires inverting the acquisition model while accounting for the noise www. Figure 12.1 uses nested subsets of signed Walsh–Hadamard patterns with a fixed random pixel permutation. Each reconstruction minimizes the same wavelet-ℓ1\ell^1ℓ1 objective with its own measurements. The examples are noiseless simulations; the signed measurements correspond to centered patterns, rather than individual binary exposures.

12.2 Dual Certificate Theory and Non-Uniform Guarantees¶

12.2.1 Random Projection of Polytopes¶

For noiseless data, w=0w=0w=0, we can use the geometric characterization of (P0(Ax0))=(P0(Ax0))(\mathcal{P}^0(Ax_0))=(\mathcal{P}_0(Ax_0))(P0(Ax0​))=(P0​(Ax0​)) from Section 11.1.2. Proposition 11.1 relates identifiable sss-sparse vectors to (s−1)(s-1)(s−1)-dimensional faces of the ℓ1\ell^1ℓ1 ball B1B_1B1​ that survive projection onto AB1AB_1AB1​. Recovery thus becomes a problem of counting faces of random polytopes. For Gaussian projections, the asymptotic analysis of Donoho and Tanner distinguishes two thresholds, described by functions CAC_ACA​ and CMC_MCM​. In the proportional-growth regime, with probability tending to one as the dimensions increase,

  • Every vector x0x_0x0​ with ∣ ⁣∣x0∣ ⁣∣0⩽CA(P/N)P|\!| x_0 |\!|_0 \leqslant C_A(P/N)P∣∣x0​∣∣0​⩽CA​(P/N)P is identifiable.

  • A typical support/sign pattern with sparsity at most CM(P/N)PC_M(P/N)PCM​(P/N)P is identifiable.

For illustration, at P/N=1/4P/N=1/4P/N=1/4, the weak threshold is roughly one quarter of PPP. Strong thresholds require recovery for every support/sign pattern; weak thresholds concern a typical pattern. Their precise values depend on the asymptotic regime. Figure 12.5 illustrates the two transitions numerically.

Above the weak threshold CM(P/N)PC_M(P/N)PCM​(P/N)P, a typical support/sign pattern fails to be identifiable with high probability. The sharp transition between these regimes is called a phase transition.

The function CMC_MCM​ can be computed numerically and has inverse-logarithmic decay, CM(r)≍1/log⁡(1/r)C_M(r)\asymp1/\log(1/r)CM​(r)≍1/log(1/r), as r→0r\to0r→0. Thus, in the high-compression regime, typical sparse vectors remain recoverable when their sparsity is proportional to the number of measurements, up to a logarithmic factor.

Randomized analysis of the Fuchs certificate.

For the probabilistic analysis, we specify independent entries with a common variance and a uniform Gaussian-type tail bound.

Conditioning on AIA_IAI​ fixes pFp_FpF​, while the off-support columns aja_jaj​ remain independent of this vector. The probability that ∣⟨aj,pF⟩∣|\langle a_j,p_F\rangle|∣⟨aj​,pF​⟩∣ reaches or exceeds 1 is bounded by 2exp⁡(−cP/∣ ⁣∣pF∣ ⁣∣2)2\exp(-cP/|\!| p_F |\!|^2)2exp(−cP/∣∣pF​∣∣2). A union bound over at most NNN columns gives the stated sample complexity and the strict off-support bound, by excluding ∣⟨aj,pF⟩∣⩾1|\langle a_j,p_F\rangle|\geqslant 1∣⟨aj​,pF​⟩∣⩾1.

For Gaussian entries, conditional on AIA_IAI​, these inner products are Gaussian with variance ∣ ⁣∣pF∣ ⁣∣2/P|\!| p_F |\!|^2/P∣∣pF​∣∣2/P. When s/Ps/Ps/P is small, ∣ ⁣∣pF∣ ⁣∣2|\!| p_F |\!|^2∣∣pF​∣∣2 is close to sss, so the largest of the N−sN-sN−s absolute correlations is approximately 2slog⁡(N−s)/P\sqrt{2s\log(N-s)/P}2slog(N−s)/P​. This gives the sharper leading-order Gaussian threshold P≈2slog⁡NP\approx2s\log NP≈2slogN.

Rotational invariance makes this statement more precise:

Ps∣ ⁣∣pF∣ ⁣∣2∼χP−s+12.\frac{Ps}{|\!| p_F |\!|^2}\sim\chi^2_{P-s+1}.∣∣pF​∣∣2Ps​∼χP−s+12​.

To see this, rotate the sss columns so that sI/ss_I/\sqrt ssI​/s​ becomes the first coordinate vector. The inverse of the corresponding diagonal entry of (G∗G)−1(G^*G)^{-1}(G∗G)−1, for G=PAIG=\sqrt P A_IG=P​AI​, is the squared distance of the first column of GGG to the span of the remaining columns. This is a chi-square variable with P−s+1P-s+1P−s+1 degrees of freedom. Thus ∣ ⁣∣pF∣ ⁣∣⩽(1+δ)s|\!| p_F |\!|\leqslant(1+\delta)\sqrt s∣∣pF​∣∣⩽(1+δ)s​ with high probability when s/Ps/Ps/P is sufficiently small and PPP is large; the factor must exceed one.

In a Gaussian asymptotic regime with s/P→0s/P\to0s/P→0, the leading-order scaling is

P≳2slog⁡(2N/ε),(12.8)P\gtrsim2s\log(2N/\varepsilon), \tag{12.8}P≳2slog(2N/ε),(12.8)

with slack needed for a finite-sample probability bound. The unspecified constant in Theorem 12.3 applies to general sub-Gaussian ensembles; it should not be identified with this Gaussian leading constant.

This is a nonuniform guarantee: the vector x0x_0x0​ is fixed before the matrix AAA is drawn. The RIP theory in Section 12.3 gives a single event on which recovery holds for all sparse vectors simultaneously.

12.3 RIP Theory for Uniform Guarantees¶

12.3.1 Restricted Isometry Constants¶

Theorem 12.5

For 0<δ<10<\delta<10<δ<1 and 1⩽s⩽N1\leqslant s\leqslant N1⩽s⩽N, if AAA is a normalized sub-Gaussian matrix and

P⩾Cδ−2slog⁡(eN/s)(12.10)P \geqslant C \delta^{-2} s \log(eN/s) \tag{12.10}P⩾Cδ−2slog(eN/s)(12.10)

it satisfies δs⩽δ\delta_s \leqslant\deltaδs​⩽δ with probability at least 1−2e−δ2P2C1 - 2e^{ -\delta^2 \frac{P}{2C} }1−2e−δ22CP​, where CCC depends only on the sub-Gaussian parameters in (12.6).

The proof combines concentration on each support with a union bound over supports.

The RIP condition (12.9) is equivalent to the spectral bound eig(AI∗AI)⊂[1−δs,1+δs]\text{eig}( A_I^* A_I ) \subset [1-\delta_s,1+\delta_s]eig(AI∗​AI​)⊂[1−δs​,1+δs​] for every column submatrix AIA_IAI​ with ∣I∣⩽s|I|\leqslant s∣I∣⩽s. For Gaussian matrices, Section 12.2.2 provides these estimates for B∗B∈Rs×sB^*B\in\mathbb{R}^{s\times s}B∗B∈Rs×s, where B∈RP×sB\in\mathbb{R}^{P\times s}B∈RP×s has independent N(0,1/P)\mathcal{N}(0,1/P)N(0,1/P) entries. The concentration bound (12.1) controls δs\delta_sδs​ on each support. Analogous nonasymptotic estimates hold under the stated sub-Gaussian assumptions; finite covariance alone would not suffice.

For a fixed support, the smallest eigenvalue is close to (1−s/P)2(1-\sqrt{s/P})^2(1−s/P​)2, a deficit of 2s/P−s/P2\sqrt{s/P}-s/P2s/P​−s/P from 1. Thus a fixed tolerance requires PPP to scale with sss. A union bound over all supports adds the logarithmic factor. This step requires nonasymptotic concentration, which the Marchenko–Pastur limit alone does not provide.

These sufficient bounds on restricted isometry constants are commonly referred to as restricted isometry properties (RIP).

The numerical constants in elementary RIP bounds can be conservative, so the resulting sufficient sample sizes may exceed the observed phase-transition thresholds.

12.3.3 RIP Implies Stable Recovery¶

For uniform stability, it is convenient to use the noise-constrained formulation (Pε(y)\mathcal {P}^\varepsilon (y)Pε(y)). The standard robust RIP estimate [6], together with Theorem 12.5, gives the following statement.

Theorem 12.8

Let 1⩽s⩽N1\leqslant s\leqslant N1⩽s⩽N and let AAA be a normalized sub-Gaussian matrix. There are constants C,c,C0,C1>0C,c,C_0,C_1>0C,c,C0​,C1​>0, depending only on its sub-Gaussian parameters, such that if

P⩾Cslog⁡(eN/s),(12.13)P\geqslant Cs\log(eN/s), \tag{12.13}P⩾Cslog(eN/s),(12.13)

then, with probability at least 1−2e−cP1-2e^{-cP}1−2e−cP, the following holds simultaneously for every x0∈RNx_0\in\mathbb{R}^Nx0​∈RN, every ε⩾0\varepsilon\geqslant 0ε⩾0, every noise vector www with ∣ ⁣∣w∣ ⁣∣⩽ε|\!| w |\!|\leqslant\varepsilon∣∣w∣∣⩽ε, and every minimizer xεx_\varepsilonxε​ of (Pε(y)\mathcal {P}^\varepsilon (y)Pε(y)) with y=Ax0+wy=Ax_0+wy=Ax0​+w:

∣ ⁣∣xε−x0∣ ⁣∣⩽C0ε+C1∣ ⁣∣x0−x0,s∣ ⁣∣1s.|\!| x_\varepsilon-x_0 |\!|\leqslant C_0\varepsilon+ C_1\frac{|\!| x_0-x_{0,s} |\!|_1}{\sqrt s}.∣∣xε​−x0​∣∣⩽C0​ε+C1​s​∣∣x0​−x0,s​∣∣1​​.

Here x0,sx_{0,s}x0,s​ is a best sss-term approximation. In particular, exactly sss-sparse vectors are recovered with error at most C0εC_0\varepsilonC0​ε, and uniquely when ε=0\varepsilon=0ε=0.

The penalized formulation also admits linear noise-error bounds: combine Theorem 12.6 with Theorem 11.11 and choose λ\lambdaλ accordingly. The bounds hold for every minimizer, but do not assert uniqueness of noisy Lasso solutions. For approximately sparse vectors, the constrained estimate measures the ℓ1\ell^1ℓ1 approximation tail divided by s\sqrt ss​, without an additional factor ∣ ⁣∣A∣ ⁣∣|\!| A |\!|∣∣A∣∣.

The order of the quantifiers distinguishes uniform from nonuniform recovery. In the noiseless case, this theorem bounds the probability of a single event on which every sss-sparse vector is recovered. Theorem 12.3 instead bounds the recovery probability separately for each vector fixed independently of AAA.

For uniform norm recovery, RIP analysis replaces log⁡N\log NlogN by log⁡(eN/s)\log(eN/s)log(eN/s). The Fuchs analysis using ηF\eta_FηF​ addresses an additional question: stability of the support. The guarantees also differ in their constants. Elementary RIP estimates can be conservative, while Gaussian fixed-signal calculations give a sharp leading constant in their asymptotic regime.

The uniform certificate constructed above need not coincide with the Fuchs precertificate ηF\eta_FηF​.

12.3.4 RIP for Fourier Sampling¶

Fully independent random measurements can be difficult to implement. A practical alternative is to sample a random subset of coefficients in an orthonormal basis Ξ=(ξω)ω=1N\Xi = (\xi_\omega)_{\omega=1}^NΞ=(ξω​)ω=1N​ of RN\mathbb{R}^NRN or CN\mathbb{C}^NCN:

Ax:=N/P (⟨x, ξω⟩)ω∈Ω(12.14)A x \mathrel{:=}\sqrt{N/P}\,( \langle x,\,\xi_\omega\rangle )_{\omega\in \Omega} \tag{12.14}Ax:=N/P​(⟨x,ξω​⟩)ω∈Ω​(12.14)

The factor N/P\sqrt{N/P}N/P​ makes the expected Gram matrix the identity. For a complex basis, the measurements are complex. The index set Ω⊂{1,…,N}\Omega\subset\{1,\ldots,N\}Ω⊂{1,…,N} is sampled uniformly without replacement, with ∣Ω∣=P|\Omega|=P∣Ω∣=P.

The following theorem gives an RIP guarantee when the basis vectors are sufficiently spread out, as quantified by

ρ(Ξ):=Nmax⁡1⩽ω⩽N  ∣ ⁣∣ξω∣ ⁣∣∞.\rho(\Xi) \mathrel{:=}\sqrt{N} \underset{1 \leqslant\omega\leqslant N}{\max}\; |\!| \xi_\omega |\!|_\infty.ρ(Ξ):=N​1⩽ω⩽Nmax​∣∣ξω​∣∣∞​.
Theorem 12.9 (Rudelson–Vershynin)

For every fixed 0<c<10<c<10<c<1 and failure exponent γ>0\gamma>0γ>0, there is a constant C=C(c,γ)C=C(c,\gamma)C=C(c,γ) such that, provided

P⩾Cρ(Ξ)2slog⁡(2N)4(12.15)P \geqslant C \rho(\Xi)^2 s \log(2N)^4 \tag{12.15}P⩾Cρ(Ξ)2slog(2N)4(12.15)

the normalized operator (12.14) satisfies δ2s⩽c\delta_{2s}\leqslant cδ2s​⩽c with probability at least 1−N−γ1-N^{-\gamma}1−N−γ.

One always has 1⩽ρ(Ξ)2⩽N1 \leqslant\rho(\Xi)^2 \leqslant N1⩽ρ(Ξ)2⩽N.

The worst case is the Dirac basis, Ξ=IdN\Xi=\mathrm{Id}_NΞ=IdN​, for which ρ(Ξ)2=N\rho(\Xi)^2=Nρ(Ξ)2=N. Indeed, uniform recovery of even one-sparse vectors then requires observing every coordinate, so P=NP=NP=N.

Fourier atoms ξω=(N−1/2e2iπNωn)n=1N∈CN\xi_\omega= (N^{-1/2}e^{\frac{2\mathrm{i}\pi}{N}\omega n} )_{n=1}^N \in \mathbb{C}^Nξω​=(N−1/2eN2iπ​ωn)n=1N​∈CN attain the smallest possible value, ρ(Ξ)=1\rho(\Xi)=1ρ(Ξ)=1; Hadamard bases do so as well. Up to logarithmic factors, the sample count (12.15) then matches the sub-Gaussian scaling (12.13).

Theorem 12.9 assumes that x0x_0x0​ is sparse in the coordinate basis. If instead f0f_0f0​ is sparse in an orthonormal basis Ψ=(ψm)m=1N\Psi=(\psi_m)_{m=1}^NΨ=(ψm​)m=1N​, use the coordinates x=Ψ∗fx = \Psi^* fx=Ψ∗f, so that xxx contains the coefficients of fff in Ψ\PsiΨ. The factor ρ(Ξ)\rho(\Xi)ρ(Ξ) in (12.15) is then replaced by the mutual coherence of the sampling and sparsity bases:

ρ(Ψ∗Ξ):=Nmax⁡1⩽ω,m⩽N  ∣⟨ψm, ξω⟩∣.\rho(\Psi^*\Xi) \mathrel{:=}\sqrt{N} \underset{1 \leqslant\omega,m \leqslant N}{\max}\; |\langle \psi_m,\,\xi_\omega\rangle|.ρ(Ψ∗Ξ):=N​1⩽ω,m⩽Nmax​∣⟨ψm​,ξω​⟩∣.

Small mutual coherence therefore yields stronger measurement bounds. Fourier and Dirac bases are maximally incoherent. Fourier and wavelet bases can have large correlations, whereas specially constructed “noiselet” bases have low coherence with suitable wavelets.

Unlike the Gaussian ensemble, these structured measurements are not universal: their recovery guarantees depend on the sparsity basis Ψ\PsiΨ.
